title: Mitigation-driven translocation effects on temperature, condition, growth, and mortality of Mojave desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) in the face of solar energy development
abstract: Given the rapid pace of renewable energy development, there is need to assess impacts of mitigation-driven translocations on sensitive species, including federally protected Mojave desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) distributed widely across a global solar energy hotspot. We monitored 215 tortoises over 3 years to evaluate translocation effects on temperature, condition, growth, and mortality of tortoises adjacent to the world's largest solar thermal plant located in southern California. On the basis of generalized estimating equation mixed models, maximum daily tortoise temperature increased with environmental temperature then leveled off at highest environmental temperatures for all three groups (translocated, resident, and control) likely due to behavioral thermoregulation. This pattern was consistent among groups, but translocated tortoises had higher average maximum daily temperature and durations above 35 °C than resident and control tortoises in the first month post-translocation, with smaller effects in the second and fourth months, and no differences in subsequent years. During the first year, adult translocated males had higher temperatures than females. Average percent changes in body condition and carapace length increased post-translocation for all groups and there were no differences in mortality probability among groups or years. Based on the relatively short-term thermal effects, and lack of negative effects on condition, growth, or mortality, our study suggests relatively minimal impacts following short-distance translocation releases in spring. Our study also serves as a unique example and first step for science-based, mitigation-driven translocations implemented to evaluate and reduce effects of translocation from solar energy development on sensitive species.

## 1. Introduction

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions by converting to renewable energy is a central part of the global effort to minimize climate change impacts on humans and biological diversity (Allison et al., 2014; Cameron et al., 2012; Hernandez et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2004). The proportion of all energy production comprised of renewable sources is expected to increase from an average of 19% worldwide in 2012 to targets as large as 100% by 2025 in certain regions or countries (REN21, 2014). In the United States, utility-scale (≥1 MW) renewable energy development has become a priority of the federal government with large-scale plans (e.g., Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan) as well as regulatory

initiatives (e.g., American Reinvestment and Recovery Act 2008; National Energy Policy Act 2005) that provide incentives for renewable sources, including solar energy, on public lands. Desert regions have high solar potential, yet also harbor sensitive species and habitats for which there is a dearth of information regarding impacts of solar development (Allison et al., 2014; Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Northrup and Wittemyer, 2013). For example, the Mojave Desert in the southwestern U.S. is a global solar energy hotspot that contains 29 species and subspecies listed as threatened or endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, while facing a boom in fast-tracked applications to develop large-scale solar facilities to supply electricity demand and meet regulatory priorities (Allison et al., 2014; Bunn et al., 2007; Cameron et al., 2012; Hernandez et al., 2015). Given the rapid pace of solar development and scarcity of scientific studies, there is an urgent need for information on impacts on sensitive species (Allison et al., 2014; Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Northrup and Wittemyer, 2013).

Where development encroaches on sensitive wildlife habitat, translocation of sensitive species to areas outside a project's footprint has been increasingly used to reduce impacts (i.e., mitigation-driven translocations), but there has remained a paucity of scientific assessments to determine effectiveness and inform future mitigation efforts worldwide (Germano et al., 2015; Northrup and Wittemyer, 2013). For example, rigorous post-release documentation following mitigation-driven translocations has been lacking for numerous threatened or endangered invertebrate, small mammal, amphibian, and reptiles species in the United States, Europe, Australia, and South America (Germano et al., 2015). The few notable exceptions that have implemented scientifically-based mitigation translocation programs have yielded important insights to reduce future impacts for those species (Germano et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015), and this provides an important example for solar development given its rapid pace. The federally protected Mojave desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) is an important representative organism that can be used to evaluate effects of solar development due to its wide distribution and potential for substantial displacement across targeted areas (Averill-Murray et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2012; Lovich and Ennen, 2011). The desert tortoise is also vulnerable to exceeding its physiological limits (Morafka and Berry, 2002) and thus may be particularly sensitive to translocation in thermally extreme environments that are optimal for solar development.

A few studies have addressed the effects of translocation on this threatened reptile (Drake et al., 2012; Esque et al., 2010; Field et al., 2007; Hinderle et al., 2015; Nussear et al., 2012), but only one has addressed mitigation-driven translocation effects on desert tortoises following utility-scale solar development (Farnsworth et al., 2015). Prior studies indicated tortoise movements increased initially post-translocation, after which tortoises established home ranges, movement behavior, or space-use indistinguishable from control tortoises (Farnsworth et al., 2015; Field et al., 2007; Nussear et al., 2012). Increased movement was likely due to either homing to familiar areas (Hinderle et al., 2015) or questing after shelter, food, or mates in unfamiliar areas, and Sullivan et al. (2015) suggested translocations have a low success rate when judged by increased movement. Translocation to unfamiliar areas may reduce the ability of individuals to locate burrows or other cover sites important for thermoregulation, and could have negative consequences on body temperature, condition, growth, or mortality (Berry, 1986; Bulova, 2002; Field et al., 2007). Behavioral thermoregulation, during which tortoises retreat into burrows to regulate body temperature and avoid water loss, is an important coping mechanism in the face of potentially lethal summer temperatures that could impact tortoises differently on the basis of gender or age (Bulova, 2002; Harless et al., 2009; Morafka and Berry, 2002; Naegle, 1976; Rautenstrauch et al., 2002; Zimmerman et al., 1994). Growth, condition, or survival could also be reduced if affected tortoises are under greater thermal stress (Field et al., 2007; Nagy et al., 2002). Given the potential risks for animals exposed to extreme temperatures, information is needed to assess these potential effects of mitigation-driven translocation on desert tortoise in the face of expanding solar development.

We investigated desert tortoise temperature, condition, growth, and mortality (the converse of survival) following translocation from the largest solar thermal plant in the world, the Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System (ISEGS) in southern California, which is capable of producing N 390 MW at capacity. Mitigation-driven translocations have been criticized for lack of planning (Germano et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015), and several important mitigation design elements were applied at this project site in an attempt to reduce impacts. For example, tortoises found within the project footprint were translocated short-distances (i.e., b500 m) to retain a putative portion of original home ranges, and during spring when environmental temperatures were lower than summer (USFWS, 2011). Importantly, these project design elements were intended to increase affected tortoise's familiarity with cover sites and reduce their exposure to extreme environmental temperatures. Our goal was to evaluate potential impacts during the hottest

– daily and seasonal periods in the first three years (2012 2014) following translocation. Our specific objectives were to 1) evaluate whether maximum tortoise temperatures and duration above threshold temperatures were higher in translocated than resident or control groups, after accounting for environmental temperature and individual tortoise characteristics; 2) evaluate how long this effect lasted post-translocation; 3) assess whether there were differences by groups within age and gender classes; and 4) assess the influence of translocation on tortoise condition, growth, and mortality. Our study provides a novel example of a science-based mitigation-driven translocation for a threatened species in the face of solar energy development.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Field data collection

We conducted our study in the Ivanpah Valley in southern California, approximately 75 km southwest of Las Vegas, NV (Fig. 1). Elevation in – the study area ranged from 790 1830 m, and vegetation consisted of Mojave desert scrub dominated by creosote bush (Larrea tridentata) and white bursage (Ambrosia dumosa). Average annual precipitation was approximately 20.1 cm, with highest rainfall during winter and a – – second pulse in July August (1981 2010; Global Historical Climatology Network station USC00267369, Searchlight, NV).

We established three study groups: translocated, resident, and control. Translocated tortoises initially occurred on the ISEGS project footprint and were translocated into the adjacent, resident population in the release area (Fig. 1). We sampled control tortoises from two subareas that encompassed a range of elevation, vegetation, and other habitat attributes present in the release area and across the Ivanpah Valley (Farnsworth et al., 2015; Fig. 1).

Biologists permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Service (8-8-10-F-24R) and the California Energy Commission (07-AFC-5C) collected tortoises beginning in October 2010 and assessed health status in quarantine pens where they were supplemented with natural vegetation and water. Tortoises that were antibody negative to two pathenogenic species that cause upper respiratory tract disease (Mycoplasma agassizii and Mycoplasma testudineum; Brown et al., 2004) tested using diagnostic enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA; USFWS, 2011), and had reached midline carapace length (MCL) N 120 mm, were translocated within two weeks of 15 April 2012. This date was chosen to reduce potential thermal stress during the coolest part of the active season. To help insure that tortoises were hydrated upon release, all tortoises were soaked in water for 1 h the day before translocation and were either offered water for intake via the nares or were administered fluids via epicoelomic injection on the day of release (USFWS, 2011). Translocated tortoises were then moved to locations b 500 m from an estimated centroid of their home range, based on each tortoise's unique tracking history during clearance surveys, then placed under shrubs characteristic of a ‘hard’ release (USFWS, 2011). Biologists captured, measured, and radio-tagged resident and control tortoises during spring and fall 2011 (Boarman et al., 1998). All tortoises were fitted with very high frequency (VHF) radio transmitters (Holohil Systems Ltd., Ontario, Canada) on initial detection for resident and control tortoises and on the day before release for translocated tortoises. Fence lines were furnished with artificial shade structures and monitored daily during spring 2012 which enabled biologists to intervene if a tortoise showed signs of distress while pacing a fence.

Of 351 tracked tortoises within resident, translocation, and control groups, we fit a random subset of 215 tortoises with temperature loggers. We classified tortoises into three age and gender classes based on size and secondary sexual characteristics: adult (MCL ≥ 180 mm) female, adult male, or immature (MCL b 180 mm). We balanced age and gender characteristics within resident and control groups to match those in the translocation group to the extent possible. We tracked tortoises with temperature loggers between April 2012 and September

2014. These included 55 translocated tortoises (20 male, 23 female, and 12 immature), 73 residents (34 male, 34 female, and 5 immature), and 87 control tortoises (35 male, 36 female, and 16 immature). We tracked tortoises approximately weekly during the five-month active season – (15 April to 15 September) spanning three years (2012 2014). We defined months as the period beginning on the 15th day of each month through the 14th of the subsequent month.

We handled tortoises during bi-yearly health assessments in May and September of each sampling year. During these six health assessments, we assessed tortoise characteristics, including MCL, gender, body condition, and antibody status. We calculated body condition (g/ cm[3] ) to characterize the nutritional and hydration status of tortoises by dividing the tortoise body mass by the product of MCL, carapace height and width (Nagy et al., 2002; USFWS, 2011). We measured initial, pre-voided body mass (g) using a Pesola spring scale, then subtracted temperature logger and radiotransmitter weights for each individual that together comprised b 5% of body mass. During health assessments we collected blood to assess antibody status of the two Mycoplasma spp. with ELISA following established protocols (USFWS, 2011), and classified tortoises as antibody positive or suspect versus negative for both pathogens. We generated variables for antibody status, condition, and MCL as time-specific variables pertaining to baseline (earlyseason 2012) and end-of-season measures for each year.

We used temperature data loggers (Thermochron iButton® DS1922L; width 1.6 cm, height 0.5 cm, weight b 3 g) to record date, time, and temperature (°C) at 15 min intervals during the active season. Our goal was to approximate cloacal temperatures of tortoises when attaching temperature loggers, and Nussear et al. (2002) found that measurements above the tail were the least different from cloacal temperatures. However, given the larger range in size and morphology of tortoises in our study, and difference in logger design, we could not consistently place the logger in this region without rubbing the skin surface. Thus, we placed loggers on the first costal scute for all tortoises when possible, or on the fourth costal or fifth vertebral scutes as necessary for immature tortoises or those with damaged keratin. To mimic the

natural tortoise surface, and to reduce potential abrasion against burrows or potential visual cues for predators, we used copper colored putty epoxy (Devcon® ITW 70345) to cover the top and side of each logger, leaving only two small holes to allow contact with the temperature probe. We downloaded loggers using a Hewlett Packard IPAQ 110 running Scanning Devices Thermochron software that connected to an iConnection device via bluetooth.

We used the same type of logger to measure comparative environmental temperature in full sun at 30 min intervals. We placed loggers on structures comprised of a concrete form stake, into which we fit an aluminum rod bent at 90° to provide a horizontal attachment on a wooden dowel in direct sun. We attached loggers approximately 7 cm above the ground surface to approximate the mid-body height of a standing tortoise. We deployed four loggers in the control area and three in the release area.

## 2.2. Statistical analysis

We were interested in maximum daily temperatures expected to induce greatest thermal stress to tortoises (Zimmerman et al., 1994), and developed two response variables defined at the unit of tortoise-day: maximum tortoise temperature and duration (in minutes) over which tortoises exceeded a 35 °C threshold temperature. We selected the 35 °C threshold based on Zimmerman et al. (1994) and by inspecting thermal profiles from penned tortoises in semi-natural conditions which suggested that as a daily preferred maximum. We calculated durations by summing the number of minutes from the midpoint interval before and after each temperature recording. We screened the data and removed partial days, (e.g., from the first and last days of temperature sampling and temporary equipment failures), to avoid biasing variables. Additionally, eight of 215 tortoises were missing during some portion of the study and 19 tortoises died. For each tortoise that died, we used the reported time-since-death estimated by biologists on weekly encounters, as well as logger data taken at 15-minute intervals, to remove records that showed no behavioral thermoregulation after death.

We were also interested in daily maximum environmental temperatures (Zimmerman et al., 1994), and collapsed the data by day, area (release versus control), and fixed sampling locations. Using linear regression, we found negligible differences among sampling locations within areas after accounting for date, so averaged by area. We screened the data for outliers and removed partial days as above for tortoise temperatures.

We used cross-sectional time-series analysis implemented in generalized estimating equations (GEE), in which we defined sampling date as the repeated measures time-series variable and tortoise as a subject-level random effect (Hardin and Hilbe, 2003; Liang and Zeger, 1986; McCullagh and Nelder, 1989; Wooldridge, 2009). We specified the exchangeable working correlation matrix and set the scale parameter equal to deviance divided by the residual degrees of freedom. This approach is appropriate for time-series data, is robust to a non-parametric residual distribution, and accounts for inherent differences among individual tortoises. Additionally, we used the Huber-White sandwich estimator (White, 1994) to obtain robust estimates of standard errors. We conducted the analysis using the ‘xtreg’ command with the ‘pa’ option in STATA 11.0 statistical analysis software (StataCorp, 2009).

We evaluated several model specifications. First, we developed a base temperature effects model that allowed a quadratic relationship between tortoise temperature and environmental temperature separately by group (translocation, resident, and control). In these base models we also included tortoise variables (age/gender, condition, and antibody status) to adjust for different mixes of tortoise' characteristics by group in the early season within a given year. Our goal with this approach was to investigate group as the causal variable (Textor et al., 2011) after appropriately adjusting for the influence of environmental temperature and tortoise characteristics that could be collinear with a group effect.

We considered several additional specifications to extend our base model. First, to assess whether tortoise temperature changed differently over years depending on group, we added a year main effect and group by year interaction to predictor variables in our base model assessed over the three years. Second, to assess whether tortoise temperature differed over a finer temporal scale (months), we added a month main effect and group by month interaction to our base model assessed separately by year. Finally, to determine if tortoise temperature varied by demographic class (adult female, adult male, and immature), we added age/gender class main effects and group by class interaction to our base model assessed separately by year.

Prior to analysis, we centered continuous variables by subtracting the mean values for maximum daily environmental temperature, its quadratic term, body condition, and carapace length. We used adult male and negative antibody status as reference categories and generated dummy variables for each main effect (group, year, month, and age/ gender class) and interaction terms with group. We used the post-estimation ‘lincom’ command to compute means, standard errors, and confidence intervals of linear combinations of coefficients (StataCorp, 2009). We interpreted coefficients relative to mean environmental temperature and for average tortoise condition with negative antibody status, and assessed significant effects among coefficients based on nonoverlapping 95% confidence intervals (CI).

In addition to temperature variables, we examined if post-translocation changes in body condition, growth, or mortality were affected by group. For condition and growth we calculated average percent change – as the end-of-season value by year (2012 2014) minus baseline (early season 2012) divided by baseline. We assessed change in body condition and carapace length as a function of group, year, and group by year interactions, after adjusting for baseline condition, carapace length, and antibody status using GEE analysis of covariance. To estimate probability of mortality we used multistate, capture-recapture models that included year, group, as well as group by year interactions (Devineau et al., 2014). We evaluated the support for mortality models using Akaike's information criterion adjusted for small sample size (AICC)

and Akaike weights (wi) and averaged estimates for groups and years across models (Burnham and Anderson, 2002). We again assessed significant effects among coefficients based on non-overlapping 95% CIs.

## 3. Results

Daily maximum tortoise temperature increased with daily maximum environmental temperature, and then leveled off at highest environmental temperatures for all three groups (Fig. 2). This consistent pattern allowed us to assess shifts in the intercept for tortoise temperature as a function of year, month, and age/gender classes, after adjusting for environmental temperature and the different mix of age and gender,

We found significant differences between group and year for both temperature outcome variables. Tortoises in the translocation group had significantly higher average maximum daily temperature (36.8 °C, 36.5–37.0 °C; mean, 95% CI) compared with resident (35.9 °C, 35.6– – 36.2 °C) and control (35.9 °C, 35.7 36.2 °C) tortoises in the first year post-translocation (Fig. 3). Similarly, translocated tortoises spent longer – (113, 102 124 min; mean, 95% CI) above the 35 °C threshold compared – – with resident (76, 64 88 min) and control tortoises (84, 73 94 min) in the first year post-translocation (Fig. 3). There were no meaningful differences among groups in the second or third years post-translocation (Fig. 3).

At a finer temporal resolution (by month), translocated tortoises had significantly higher maximum daily temperatures (37.1 °C, 36.7–37.5 ° C; mean, 95% CI) than resident (34.8 °C, 34.2–35.4 °C) and control – (33.7 °C, 33.0 34.4 °C) tortoises in the first month (Fig. 4). This effect continued into the second month but with smaller differences among groups, after which there were no meaningful differences among groups in the third through fifth months post-translocation during the first year (Fig. 4), and no differences in maximum tortoise temperature among groups within any month in the second or third years posttranslocation. Translocated tortoises also spent an average of about 2.5 – times longer above 35 °C (138, 120 155 min; mean, 95% CI) than resident (51, 35–67 min) and control (57, 46–69 min) tortoises in the first month. Translocated tortoises showed a smaller effect in the second and fourth months, but there were no differences among groups in third and fifth months of the first year (Fig. 4). Neither translocated nor resident tortoises had increased duration above 35 °C compared with control tortoises in any month during the 2013 or 2014 active seasons (Fig. 4). Male translocated tortoises had significantly higher daily maximum temperature and duration N 35 °C compared with resident and control males in the first but not second and third-year post-translocation, with the exception of translocated versus control tortoises in 2014 (Fig. 5). Female translocated tortoises also had higher maximum temperature but with smaller differences among groups in the first year and no meaningful differences in subsequent years, and with fewer differences in duration N35 °C (Fig. 5). In contrast to the adults, resident immature tortoises had significantly higher maximum temperature and duration N 35 °C than translocated and control groups in the first year; there were few differences among immature groups in 2013– 2014 (Fig. 5).

Changes in growth and body condition increased on average after the 2012 baseline but with no significant differences among translocated, resident, and control groups. Percent change in carapace length was negatively related with baseline carapace length (slope = − 1.34, SE = 0.07, t = − 19.1, P b 0.0001), indicating less growth for larger than smaller tortoises. After accounting for this effect, average percent change in carapace length from 2012 baseline increased 0.9–1.2% by end-of-season 2012, 3.9–4.5% by end-of-season 2013, and 5.8–7.1% by end-of-season 2014 (Fig. 6). Percent change in body condition was also related with baseline body condition (slope = −65.3, SE = 8.8, t = −7.44, P b 0.0001), indicating reduced changes in condition for tortoises that were already better condition. After accounting for this effect, average percent change in body condition from baseline increased 6.7–7.5% by end-of-season 2012, 11.0– – 12.9% by end-of-season 2013, and 12.4 14.4% by end-of-season 2014 (Fig. 6).

## 4. Discussion

Mitigation-driven translocations are being permitted rapidly for solar energy development in desert regions, despite a paucity of science-based assessments of impacts to sensitive species (Cameron et al., 2012; Germano et al., 2015; Lovich and Ennen, 2011). Given available information, Sullivan et al. (2015) suggested a high failure rate for mitigation translocations of reptiles, which they attributed to both lack of pre-translocation planning and increased movement by animals translocated far from original home ranges. Despite translocating

Fig. 7. Probability of mortality by study group and year, within the first (2012), second (2013), and third year (2014) post-translocation. Error bars are 95% CIs for which we assessed significant effects among groups and years.

tortoises closer to original home ranges in our study, translocated individuals increased movement during their first year, after which movement was indistinguishable from control and resident tortoises in subsequent years (Farnsworth et al., 2015). Nevertheless, it has been unclear what ultimate effect this temporary movement may have, and we investigated changes in body temperature, condition, growth, and mortality following short-distance translocation.

Desert tortoises evolved in more mesic climates and depend upon physiological and behavioral exaptations, including burrow excavation, to survive in extreme heat and low moisture (Morafka and Berry, 2002). We observed an increase in tortoise temperature with increasing environmental temperature, then leveling off at highest environmental temperatures, which likely corresponds with use of burrows to behaviorally thermoregulate (Bulova, 1994, 2002; Rautenstrauch et al., 2002; Zimmerman et al., 1994). This pattern was consistent across all three groups, but with higher maximum daily temperatures and longer duration above 35 °C for translocated than resident and control tortoises, particularly during the first month post-translocation. Possible causes of these temperature effects include exploration of new habitat and establishment of territories. Additionally, Hinderle et al. (2015) found that 44% of tortoises translocated short-distances (≤2-km) attempted to return home. Similarly in this study, several tortoises were observed pacing project fencing particularly within the first few weeks (A.F.S., personal observation). This behavior increased temperature effects only temporarily, however, since these effects were reduced in the sec– ond month and were largely gone by months 3 5 and during the entire second and third years post-translocation.

The relatively short-term thermal effects may have been ameliorated, in part, by tortoise familiarity with cover site locations or because tortoises were released with time to find or construct burrows during cooler environmental temperatures in spring (Henen, 1997; Nussear et al., 2012). Even highest translocated tortoise temperatures in the first month were within the range of variation for all groups later in the active season. Tortoise temperatures were highest during mid-July to mid-September in all study groups in all years, co-occurring with both high environmental temperatures and a pulse of precipitation and green-up of summer annuals characteristic of the east Mojave Desert, during which tortoises likely increased activity to drink and forage (Duda et al., 1999; Oftedal, 2002).

Translocated males had higher temperatures than females during the first year, perhaps due to establishment of larger home ranges or a greater number of deep burrows used by males during summer (Harless et al., 2009; Rautenstrauch et al., 2002). Immature tortoises showed the opposite pattern from adults with higher temperatures for residents compared with translocated or control tortoises. While this pattern suggests that translocation may impact thermal regulatory behavior of resident immature tortoises, the mechanisms are unknown and sample size of resident immature tortoises was small (n = 5). Thus this pattern may reflect sampling variability unrelated with group, such as destruction of the immature's burrows by rain or trampling. Immature tortoises may be more vulnerable to exposure, given greater loss of body mass from evaporation for neonates than adults (Wilson et al., 2001), but confirmation in other studies is needed to assess the generality and potential causes of this pattern for resident immature tortoises.

Despite short-term temperature effects, there were no apparent negative effects of translocation on body condition, growth, or mortality following translocation. Average change in condition was positive during the first active season for all groups, in contrast to Nagy et al. (2002) that found condition declined over the active season in a year following high winter rainfall across the east and west Mojave Desert. The improved body condition we observed followed a low rainfall winter (November 2011 to April 2012) that was only 20% (0.98 in.) of average during 1981–2010 (4.59 in.). Increased average change in body condition each year likely reflected increased hydration status of tortoises from availability of green forage plants or rainwater for drinking (Nagy et al., 2002; Oftedal, 2002). That body condition improved in

– 2013 and 2014 compared with 2012 may also reflect July August precipitation that was greater in those years (5.48 in. in 2013 and 1.87 in 2014, compared with 0.62 in. in 2012). In addition to improved body condition, tortoises in all three study groups increased carapace length each year by approximately 6% by the third-year. Field et al. (2007) found that water supplementation for captive tortoises prior to translocation was correlated with high rates of carapace growth. Likewise, increased precipitation could have contributed to increased tortoise growth in our study. Additionally, translocated tortoises may have benefited from water supplementation prior to release that perhaps compensated for short-term elevated body temperatures during the first months and minimized differences in mortality among groups.

There has been skepticism about impacts of mitigation-driven translocations on sensitive species in desert regions (Germano et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015), and several studies have evaluated desert tortoises translocated following exurban or military development. These studies have found no effect of translocation compared with resident or control populations on survivorship or mortality (Esque et al., 2010; Field et al., 2007; Nussear et al., 2012), stress (Drake et al., 2012), or reproductive output (Nussear et al., 2012). Increased movement has been the largest effect observed in both long-distance (Field et al., 2007; Nussear et al., 2012) and short-distance (Farnsworth et al., 2015; Hinderle et al., 2015) translocations. For short-distance translocations, we observed short-term thermal effects primarily in the first month but no differences in condition, growth or mortality for translocated tortoises. Several authors have suggested translocation of desert tortoises may serve as a conservation or mitigation tool (Drake et al., 2012; Field et al., 2007; Nussear et al., 2012), and given the lack of group effects on condition, growth, or mortality, our study supports these previous findings.

## 5. Conclusions

Given climate change threats to biodiversity, renewable energy serves as part of the strategy to minimize impacts by reducing carbon emissions (Cameron et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2004). Allison et al. (2014) suggested that the speed and scale of renewable energy development required to reduce the worst effects of global warming precludes exhaustive research to assess impacts on all wildlife species potentially affected. Science-based mitigation-driven translocations can provide a template in which repeated monitoring efforts applied to individual developments can feed into retrospective meta-analyses and adaptive management efforts, to iteratively identify ecological and management factors needed to minimize impacts between development and wildlife (Germano et al., 2015). Our study, combined with Farnsworth et al. (2015), provides a unique example and first step for science-based, mitigation-driven translocations applied in the context of expanding solar and other renewable energy development.

Utility-scale solar energy development has one of the greatest potentials for climate change mitigation among renewables, but requires large areas to concentrate solar energy that can induce conservation, regulatory, and legal conflicts with threatened and endangered species (Badichek, 2015; Hernandez et al., 2015; Lovich and Ennen, 2011). Solar siting in areas of low conservation value is the first step in a mitigation hierarchy, but if translocation of sensitive species cannot be avoided, then projects should be carefully planned to reduce impacts (Allison et al., 2014; Cameron et al., 2012; Hernandez et al., 2015).

Our findings suggest implications for future mitigation-driven translocations for the desert tortoise, a species on the front-line of development in a global solar energy hotspot. Given the relatively short-term thermal effects we observed, our study supports use of short-distance translocation releases in spring, which may have reduced thermal effects due to familiarity with cover locations during a season with lower temperatures and relatively abundant food and water resources (Henen, 1997; Oftedal, 2002). Our study also suggests the importance of shade structures and monitoring along project fencing in the first month post-release to reduce thermal exposure for individual tortoises

attempting to home, particularly for short-distance translocations (Hinderle et al., 2015). To further reduce thermal stress, mitigations should ensure suitable habitat for translocated animals, such as adequate shrub cover and loamy soils, that allow tortoises to most easily find shelter and dig burrows (Andersen et al., 2000). Habitat might be enhanced by providing artificial burrows in a ‘soft’ rather than ‘hard’ release. The lack of translocation effects we observed on condition, growth, and mortality suggests potential use of short-distance translocation in a region with precipitation characteristic of the east Mojave Desert. Further research is needed in regions with drier climate, including those that lack summer rains such as the western Mojave Desert, and particularly in the face of drought or warming climate (Abatzoglou and Kolden, 2011; Lovich et al., 2014). Our study serves as an example for other regions and countries working to minimize impact between solar energy development and species of concern using science-based, mitigation-driven translocations.
